This tutorial uses the complete-case National Health and Nutrition Examination
Survey I Epidemiologic Follow-up Study (NHEFS) data distributed through the
`causaldata` example-data package and mirrored by RDatasets.

The causal question is:

```text
What is the effect of quitting smoking on weight change from 1971 to 1982?
```

This is a more realistic example than a randomized job-training graph. The
treatment is not randomized, so identification depends on assumptions about
baseline confounding by demographics, education, smoking history, activity, and
baseline weight.

## Setup

```{julia}
import Pkg
Pkg.activate(joinpath(@__DIR__, ".."); io=devnull)

using CausalGraphs
using DataFrames
using DelimitedFiles
using Downloads
using Printf
```

## 1. Load NHEFS Complete-Case Data

The outcome is `wt82_71`, weight change from 1971 to 1982. The treatment is
`qsmk`, an indicator for quitting smoking between the baseline questionnaire
and follow-up.

```{julia}
function read_rdatasets_csv(url, cols)
    local_file = Downloads.download(url; timeout=120)
    x, header = readdlm(local_file, ',', Any, '\n'; header=true)
    raw = DataFrame(x, Symbol.(vec(header)))
    DataFrame((c => Float64.(raw[!, c]) for c in cols)...)
end

url = "https://vincentarelbundock.github.io/Rdatasets/csv/causaldata/nhefs_complete.csv"

cols = [
    :qsmk, :wt82_71,
    :sex, :race, :age, :school,
    :smokeintensity, :smokeyrs,
    :exercise, :active, :wt71,
]

data = read_rdatasets_csv(url, cols)

println("n = ", nrow(data))
first(data, 5)
```

## 2. Hypothesize a Causal Graph

In an observational analysis, this graph is not learned from the data and it is
not known to be true. It is a compact statement of assumptions. Those
assumptions would usually come from temporal ordering, subject-matter knowledge,
the study protocol, prior literature, and discussion with domain experts.

For this example, the clean conceptual graph is just an adjustment DAG:

```text
X -> A -> Y
X -----> Y
```

where `X` is the baseline covariate set, `A` is quitting smoking, and `Y` is
later weight change. We use `A` rather than `M` because quitting is the treatment
here. A node called `M` would usually be a mediator between treatment and
outcome.

```{julia}
conceptual_graph = make_graph(
    vertices=[:X, :A, :Y],
    di_edges=[(:X, :A), (:X, :Y), (:A, :Y)],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(conceptual_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

This grouped graph states the minimal structure needed for the example:

1. The baseline variables were measured before quitting status and before later
   weight change.
2. Each baseline variable is allowed to affect quitting, later weight change, or
   both.
3. Quitting may affect later weight change.
4. There is no unmeasured common cause of quitting and later weight change after
   adjusting for these baseline variables.

The fourth point is the strongest assumption. The DAG makes it visible so that
we can challenge it.

For estimation, `X` has to be expanded into the actual data columns used by the
nuisance models:

```{julia}
vertices = [
    :sex, :race, :age, :school,
    :smokeintensity, :smokeyrs,
    :exercise, :active, :wt71,
    :qsmk, :wt82_71,
]

baseline = setdiff(vertices, [:qsmk, :wt82_71])

edges = vcat(
    [(w, :qsmk) for w in baseline],
    [(w, :wt82_71) for w in baseline],
    [(:qsmk, :wt82_71)],
)

graph = make_graph(vertices=vertices, di_edges=edges);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

## 3. Identify

The identifying logic is now direct. Under this adjustment DAG, conditioning on
the measured baseline variables blocks the backdoor paths from quitting to later
weight change.

```{julia}
id = identify(graph, :qsmk, :wt82_71)
println("strategy: ", id.strategy)
println("Markov pillow of qsmk: ", markov_pillow(graph, :qsmk; treatment=:qsmk))
```

The effect is `:a_fixable`, so `estimate_causal()` routes to the backdoor
estimators.

This conclusion is conditional on the graph. If we instead believe there is an
unmeasured common cause of quitting and later weight change, we should encode
that as a bidirected edge and identify again:

```{julia}
sensitivity_graph = make_graph(
    vertices=vertices,
    di_edges=edges,
    bi_edges=[(:qsmk, :wt82_71)],
)

sensitivity_id = identify(sensitivity_graph, :qsmk, :wt82_71)
println("strategy with unmeasured qsmk-wt82_71 confounding: ",
        sensitivity_id.strategy)
```

With that extra assumption, this package reports the effect as not identified.
That is the point of drawing the DAG: it makes the identifying assumptions
explicit enough to challenge.

## 4. Estimate

```{julia}
res = estimate_causal(
    a = [1, 0],
    data = data,
    graph = graph,
    treatment = :qsmk,
    outcome = :wt82_71,
)

@printf("TMLE:    ACE = %.2f  95%% CI (%.2f, %.2f)\n",
        res[:TMLE].ACE, res[:TMLE].lower_ci, res[:TMLE].upper_ci)
@printf("Onestep: ACE = %.2f\n", res[:Onestep].ACE)
@printf("Gcomp:   ACE = %.2f\n", res[:Gcomp].ACE)
@printf("IPW:     ACE = %.2f\n", res[:IPW].ACE)
```

Interpreted under the graph, the TMLE estimate is the average effect of quitting
smoking versus continuing smoking on weight change over follow-up, in the
complete-case NHEFS population.

## Why This Example Is Useful

This example shows a more realistic applied workflow:

1. The main DAG is the simple grouped adjustment graph `X -> A -> Y` and
   `X -> Y`.
2. The graph is presented as a hypothesis, not as something recovered from the
   observed data.
3. The expanded graph is only the implementation form needed because the data
   have separate covariate columns.
4. The same workflow can compare candidate graphs before estimation.
5. Identification can disappear when a plausible unmeasured-confounding
   assumption is added.

## Alternative: Structured Baseline Model

The simple adjustment DAG is often the right place to start. If we want to make
more baseline structure explicit, we can write a richer alternative model. This
is a stronger set of assumptions, so it belongs after the simple model rather
than replacing it.

At the conceptual level, the alternative groups variables like this:

- `D`: demographics, such as sex, race, and age
- `E`: education
- `H`: smoking history
- `L`: activity and exercise
- `W`: baseline weight
- `A`: quitting smoking
- `Y`: later weight change

```{julia}
structured_conceptual_graph = make_graph(
    vertices=[:D, :E, :H, :L, :W, :A, :Y],
    di_edges=[
        (:D, :E), (:D, :H), (:D, :L), (:D, :W), (:D, :A), (:D, :Y),
        (:E, :H), (:E, :A), (:E, :Y),
        (:H, :A), (:H, :Y),
        (:L, :W), (:L, :A), (:L, :Y),
        (:W, :A), (:W, :Y),
        (:A, :Y),
    ],
);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(structured_conceptual_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

Expanded to the actual columns, one version of that model is:

```{julia}
structured_edges = [
    (:age, :school), (:age, :smokeyrs), (:age, :wt71),
    (:age, :active), (:age, :exercise), (:age, :qsmk), (:age, :wt82_71),

    (:sex, :smokeintensity), (:sex, :smokeyrs), (:sex, :wt71),
    (:sex, :qsmk), (:sex, :wt82_71),

    (:race, :school), (:race, :smokeintensity),
    (:race, :qsmk), (:race, :wt82_71),

    (:school, :smokeintensity), (:school, :qsmk), (:school, :wt82_71),

    (:smokeyrs, :smokeintensity), (:smokeyrs, :qsmk), (:smokeyrs, :wt82_71),
    (:smokeintensity, :qsmk), (:smokeintensity, :wt82_71),

    (:exercise, :wt71), (:exercise, :qsmk), (:exercise, :wt82_71),
    (:active, :wt71), (:active, :qsmk), (:active, :wt82_71),
    (:wt71, :qsmk), (:wt71, :wt82_71),

    (:qsmk, :wt82_71),
]

structured_graph = make_graph(vertices=vertices, di_edges=structured_edges);
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("```{mermaid}")
println(to_mermaid(structured_graph; direction="LR"))
println("```")
```

This richer graph gives the same identification result for the quitting effect:

```{julia}
structured_id = identify(structured_graph, :qsmk, :wt82_71)
println("strategy under structured baseline model: ", structured_id.strategy)
println("Markov pillow of qsmk: ",
        markov_pillow(structured_graph, :qsmk; treatment=:qsmk))
```

Because the structured graph gives `qsmk` the same measured baseline parents as
the simple adjustment graph, `estimate_causal()` uses the same adjustment set.
For this treatment effect, the two DAGs are adjustment-equivalent: they imply
the same sufficient adjustment set and therefore the same estimating formulas.
They are not the same full causal model, because the structured DAG also makes
claims about how baseline variables cause one another. Those extra claims do not
affect this particular backdoor adjustment.

For this estimand, the richer graph is not needed to estimate the effect. Its
value is mainly communicative: it records a more detailed causal story about how
baseline variables may relate to one another. If that story is hard to defend,
the simpler grouped adjustment DAG is preferable.
